scenes.narration: For nearly two days, Niagara Falls almost completely stopped flowing.
And nobody had turned it off.
It happened in March of 1848.
People living near the falls were used to the constant, thunderous roar of millions of gallons of water.
Then, one night, something changed.
The roar began fading.
By the next morning, people looked toward Niagara...
and saw something almost unimaginable.
The river had dropped dramatically. The mighty falls had been reduced to a trickle.
People reportedly ventured onto exposed parts of the riverbed, exploring ground that was normally buried beneath rushing water.
So where did all the water go?
The answer was sitting miles upstream.
Powerful winds had pushed huge amounts of ice across Lake Erie.
Near the entrance to the Niagara River, that ice piled together into an enormous natural dam.
The blockage became so severe that it dramatically reduced the water flowing toward the falls.
For roughly 30 hours, Niagara was eerily quiet.
But there was one obvious problem.
That water was eventually coming back.
When the winds shifted, the ice dam broke apart.
The Niagara River surged back to life...
and the famous roar returned.
Niagara Falls has been deliberately reduced or diverted since.
But in 1848, nature essentially switched off one of the world's most powerful waterfalls...
using nothing but ice.
